findings.seam: the retired section names outside packs/ -- scripts/tickets_registry.py's refusal remedy, and reader/docs/workflows.md's orch-do line
findings.summary: Two live prose surfaces still send a reader to craft sections this revision retired. One of them is a refusal message, which is a public seam: a caller holding `orch-outline`, `orch-spec`, `orch-slice` or `orch-decompose` is told the remedy is "a planning `do` reading the pack craft's Outline and Spec fields sections", and after this revision no craft has an `## Outline`.
findings.evidence: scripts/tickets_registry.py:40 (the comment) and :45-47 (`_PLANNING_DO_REMEDY`, the string `executor_successor` and `executor_refusal` both return) still read "the pack craft's Outline and Spec fields sections"; the identical literal is copied into tests/test_registry_census.py:171-173 and asserted with assertEqual, so the check passes while the fact it pins is false. reader/docs/workflows.md:22 reads "produce one artifact through the stamped pack's craft, or plan through its Outline and Spec fields sections". A git grep for the four retired headings and for "Outline and Spec fields" over tracked files returns exactly these two live surfaces plus historical records (research/lego-design-2026-08-31.md, an earlier review's quotation) and the validator's own CRAFT_RETIRED_SECTIONS machinery. B1.2 and B1.3 both flagged the tickets_registry.py half and correctly left it alone as outside their edit surface; the reader/ half is named by no unit's report.
findings.cause: The retired-heading check the run added is scoped to craft files: tools/validate_support/names.py `validate_craft_sections` iterates packages and reads `references/craft.md`, so a retired section name written in prose anywhere else is invisible to it. The migration's surface census was therefore the union of five hand-written file lists, and a fact that lives only in prose has no mechanical owner to notice when it goes stale.
findings.remedy: Smallest change, and it is small: re-key `_PLANNING_DO_REMEDY` to name the entries that now hold that content -- "a planning `do` reading the pack craft's `## Lens` `### root` or `### cut` entry and its `## Spec fields`" -- and move the identical literal in tests/test_registry_census.py:171-173 in the same commit, since the test copies the sentence rather than reading an anchor; then reword reader/docs/workflows.md:22 the same way. That is three edits and closes both sites. Extinguishing the class properly is successor scope and needs care: a blunt tree-wide grep for the four retired names would fire on the T0 supersession records and design documents that must keep quoting them, so the check wants a corpus that excludes historical records -- the shape tools/validate_support/names.py NAME_CHECKED_FILES already has.

findings.seam: the `blocking` field -- one owner, and it is a domain pack's craft (the ticket's named open item)
findings.summary: The outline says each `## Lens` entry states which findings are `blocking: true`. Only orch-code-pack's `### git` carries that paragraph. The four other deliverable entries do not, and neither does any contract, rule or skill body -- so a judge stamped with any pack but this one is told to mark findings `blocking` and has nothing anywhere to read for what the word means.
findings.evidence: A git grep for `blocking` over packs/, contracts/, rules/, skills/ and docs/ returns exactly two lines, both packs/orch-code-pack/references/craft.md:81 and :84. The same grep at 8e643085 returns the same two lines, so this is pre-existing and was neither introduced nor widened by the migration -- what changed is only which heading the paragraph sits under. rules/verification.md, which owns the critique/repair boundary, says nothing about the field. skills/kernel/orch-judge/SKILL.md instructs "Write the findings to one JSON file" without defining it, and this very ticket's Goal says "`blocking` per the craft".
findings.cause: The paragraph fuses two facts of different tiers. "A finding is blocking:true when it shows a frozen completion criterion false, or is a correctness finding at the fixed identity; contract fidelity with no criterion failing, scope and shape are blocking:false, reported never repaired in the same run" is library law about a review record's schema and about run boundaries -- true in every domain. "Weigh in this order -- a shape finding never outranks a correctness finding" is code taste, and its four counterparts differ per domain. Because the two are one paragraph, the only ways to give the four other packs the first half are to copy it four times or to leave them with nothing, and U3's Goal (text moved not rewritten, under a word budget) correctly forbade the copy.
findings.remedy: Split the paragraph at the tier line rather than fanning it out. Move the library half to the one cross-cutting owner -- rules/verification.md, which already owns what a critique returns and what a repair may touch -- and leave in each craft's deliverable Lens entry only the domain's own weighting sentence. That is one new owner plus one short clause per craft, against four copies of a paragraph, and it is the version that keeps one fact one owner. Successor scope: it is new prose in five files under word budgets, it fails none of this run's three acceptance criteria, and the craft forbids repairing a non-blocking finding in the run that reported it.

findings.seam: scripts/tickets_assignment.py `lens_key` -- artifact lines outrank `makes` with no executor gate
findings.summary: `lens_key` decides a `do`'s entry the same way it decides a judge's: if the ticket's Context carries any `- artifact:` line, that line's kind wins and `makes` is never read. A planning `do` minted `--makes root` whose Context also cited its predecessor's identity would be sent to `### git`. No supported path builds that ticket today, so nothing is wrong at this fixed identity -- but the precedence is one flag away from being wrong.
findings.evidence: scripts/tickets_assignment.py:295-302: `kinds` is collected from the Context lines first and the `if kinds:` return fires before `dequote(loaded.get(MAKES_FIELD)) or artifact_kind(...)` is reached; nothing in the function reads the executor. Called directly with {'makes':'root','pack':'orch-code-pack'} and a Context carrying `- artifact: git:b7a5f592...`, it returns `git`; with the same loaded ticket and no artifact line it returns `root`. Reachability, checked rather than assumed, and it is why this is not blocking: scripts/tickets_mint.py:401 refuses `--artifacts` on a `do` ("--artifacts belongs to judge"), so a `do` ticket leaves the mint with no artifact line; adding one afterwards fails admission -- I appended `- artifact: git:b7a5f592...` to a minted `do`'s `## Context` in a sandbox sink and `dispatch_assignment` refused with "dispatch admission grade failed"; and `tickets.py new`, which does take free-text `--context`, has no `--makes` flag, so `makes` is absent there and the fallback reaches the adapter anyway. The function's own docstring shows the intent is judge-only: "A judge is handed finished artifacts, so the typed identities on its Context name the kind it checks."
findings.cause: The docstring states a rule about judges and the code states a rule about tickets. The discriminator that would make them the same rule already exists two files away and is already read in this very prompt path -- `_files_findings(assignment)`, which U5 factored out of scripts/tickets_dispatch_launch.py precisely so the judging discriminator is read once -- but `lens_key` runs in tickets_assignment.py, before that value is available, so it inferred the executor from the data instead of asking.
findings.remedy: Gate the first branch on the executor rather than on the data: read EXECUTOR_REGISTRY[_executor_of(loaded)]['files_findings'] (tickets_assignment.py already imports `_executor_of`) and take the Context artifact lines only for a judge, falling through to `makes` then the adapter otherwise. One condition, and it makes the code say what the docstring already says. Worth doing before, not after, anything adds `--makes` to `tickets.py new` or lets a planning `do` cite a predecessor identity -- which rules/topology.md's successor clause ("cites it in the successor root's Context") points squarely at.

findings.seam: tools/validate_support/common.py CRAFT_OPTIONAL_SECTIONS -- a constant with no reader, beside a roster that is not closed
findings.summary: The `###` keys under `## Lens` are now a closed set -- a missing key and an extra key are both ERRORs. The `##` roster one level up is not: mandatory-present and retired-absent are checked, nothing else, so a craft may carry any novel `## X` and pass. The constant that names the permitted optional section, CRAFT_OPTIONAL_SECTIONS, is defined and exported and read by nothing.
findings.evidence: A tree-wide grep for CRAFT_OPTIONAL_SECTIONS returns exactly two lines, both in tools/validate_support/common.py -- the definition at :81 and the `__all__` entry at :238. The same grep at 8e643085 returns the same two lines, so the constant was already dead and U2 edited its value (from ("Shape","Stages") to ("Stages",)) without giving it a reader. tools/validate_support/names.py:158-198 shows the asymmetry directly: two loops over CRAFT_MANDATORY_SECTIONS and CRAFT_RETIRED_SECTIONS for `##`, then both a missing-key and an extra-key loop for `###`.
findings.cause: The migration closed the level it was adding and left the level it inherited. Closing `##` was never part of any unit's Goal, and the retired-section check covers the only four names that could plausibly reappear, so the gap has no current victim -- but it does leave a constant standing as if it were law.
findings.remedy: Either use it or delete it, and using it is barely larger: a third loop reporting the found headings minus mandatory, optional and retired gives the `##` roster the same closure the `###` keys have and gives the constant its reader, in about four lines. Deleting the constant and its `__all__` entry is the smaller change and is honest too. What is not acceptable is leaving both -- a named constant that no code consults reads, to the next author, as a rule that is being enforced.

findings.seam: scripts/tickets_dispatch_launch.py -- 576 to 604 lines, grown while already past the one-read band
findings.summary: U5 added the lens sentence and the factored `_files_findings` to a module that was already 76 lines past the craft's one-read band. The craft's answer to that band is to grow sideways at a seam, not to add girth.
findings.evidence: 604 physical lines at the tip against 576 at 8e643085. tools/check_source_sizes.py exits 0 with warnings=38, identical to the figure B1.5 measured at the base, and names this module: "WARN scripts\tickets_dispatch_launch.py: 604 physical lines (presumption 500)". So no ratchet regressed and no module newly crossed -- this is the presumption, which is warn-only, not the hard cap it used to be. tests/test_dispatch_launch.py is 938 lines, which B1.5 recorded and explicitly declined to split as outside Goal.
findings.cause: The unit boundary was drawn around a behavior (the prompt names the kind), and the behavior's natural home is the prompt composer, which was already oversized before this run began. Nothing in the ticket set priced the module against its bound, and the craft's cut rule that would have -- "a Goal ordering growth into a named file prices that file against the standards owner's bounds at cut time" -- is a rule for the cut, so by the time U5 read it the price was already paid.
findings.remedy: Successor scope, and there is a seam ready for it: the prompt is assembled from independent line groups (`_craft_lines`, `_return_lines`, `_files_findings` and their siblings) that share only the assignment dict. Moving the line-group builders to a `tickets_dispatch_launch_lines.py` beside the composer is a sideways move at an existing boundary, not a shave, and would take both this module and its 938-line test file back under the band together.
